label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
# My Van Almost Burned Down. Here's Every Electrical Detail I Wish I'd Known Last Month.

Last Wednesday I was in a client's driveway in Bedford with my hands in a wet Bernese Mountain Dog's armpits, dryer on high, and I smelled hot plastic.

Not "oh, the dryer's motor is warm" hot plastic. Hot plastic. The kind of smell that made my whole stomach drop before my brain caught up.

I looked down. Smoke was coming out of the bench seat where my batteries live.

Here's the whole thing. Every number, every mistake, and exactly what I'd tell you to check on your own van before it becomes my problem instead of yours.

**One thing first: I am not an electrician.** I paid a very good one to come look at my van and tell me what was wrong. Everything technical in this post is either something Priya from Sackville Marine Electric showed me, something I measured myself, or something I'm asking my builder in writing. Please don't use this as a substitute for having your own system looked at by someone who does this for a living. I would very much like to not write a sequel.

## What happened

Wednesday October 28th, around 2:15pm. Client's driveway in Bedford. Drying Moose, a Bernese Mountain Dog, on high. I was about ten minutes into the dry.

Setup:

- **Inverter:** 3000W, 12V
- **Batteries:** two 200Ah lithium, 12V
- **Built by:** Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren), spring 2025
- **Dryer:** pulls roughly 1800–2000W
- **Water heater:** sometimes on at the same time
- **Cable from battery to inverter:** 4 AWG

Timeline, because this part matters. It wasn't a sudden explosion. It was a slow-burn failure that smelled wrong for about thirty seconds before it got bad.

I smelled hot plastic first and assumed it was the dryer motor overheating because I'd been running it hard. Then I saw actual smoke coming out of the bench seat. I killed the battery switch, got Moose out the side door — he was still damp and completely thrilled about the whole thing, tail going — and used the extinguisher a bit. Honestly I still don't know if I needed to. The lug on the positive end was black and the cable jacket had melted back about 3cm from it.

Everyone's fine. Moose is fine. The client's driveway is fine. But I'm off the road for weeks, I've cancelled 31 appointments, and my whole income lives in that van.

## The part that still makes me sick

Priya pulled up the photos I took of the damage next to thermal camera shots from her own van running the same kind of load — dryer on high, same inverter, similar battery bank.

Her cables barely got warm.

Not "a little warm." *Barely.* My melted lug was a different universe from her setup running the same equipment.

And here's the thing I keep circling back to: **I trusted the build because it looked tidy.** Cables were neat, everything was wrapped, the bench looked professional. Tidy is not the same as right. Tidy is really good at hiding the exact things you need to see.

## What actually went wrong (three things, all at once)

**1. The cable was way too small for the load.**

A 3000W inverter on 12V is asking for about 250 amps when it's running at full tilt. Add my dryer pulling 1800–2000W and the water heater coming on, and here's the actual math:

| Load | Watts | Amps at 12V |
|---|---|---|
| Dryer on high | 1800W | ~150A |
| Dryer on high | 2000W | ~167A |
| Dryer + water heater | ~2800–3000W | ~233–250A |
| Inverter at full rating | 3000W | 250A |

So that 4 AWG cable was carrying somewhere between 150 and 250 amps continuously. A 4 AWG cable is generally good for around 100 amps in this kind of installation. I was pushing one-and-a-half to two-and-a-half times its rating, for as long as I was grooming.

Priya said it should have been **2/0** for a 3000W inverter at 12V. That's the cable that comes with the job.

**2. The lug was crimped wrong.**

This is the one that actually started the fire, I think. The positive lug had been crimped with pliers or a hammer instead of a proper crimping tool with the right die for that wire size. And there was heat-shrink over the top of it, which meant the bad crimp was hidden underneath.

A bad crimp has way more electrical resistance than a good one. All that extra resistance turns into heat right at that one point. So the cable was already too hot from being undersized, and then the crimp made a hot spot on top of the hot cable. The lug got hot enough to melt the jacket back off itself.

That's why I smelled plastic *before* I saw smoke. It wasn't a short that popped. It was a wire cooking itself from the inside out over a period of minutes.

**3. The fuse was too far from the battery.**

I had a 300A ANL fuse. Priya said the fuse should be mounted within about 18cm of the battery. Mine was about 90cm away.

That gap is a problem because the fuse is supposed to protect the cable. If something downstream shorts, you want the fuse to blow almost immediately. With 90cm of unprotected cable between the battery and the fuse, that entire stretch of wire has to survive the fault current before the fuse ever sees it. The wire can melt — and it did.

And here's the part I want you to really take away: **a 300A fuse on a 100A cable is not protection. It's decoration.** The fuse was never going to blow before the wire gave up, because the wire gave up first. The fuse rating and the cable rating have to make sense together, and the cable has to be sized for the load.

## The repair

**$4,200.** Rewire the main runs, new fuse block, class T fuse. Minimum three weeks, parts on order. The adjuster's coming Thursday and insurance says "maybe."

Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook. I want to remember that, actually. I was in her driveway and I was the one being taken care of, and she did that anyway.

I've cancelled 31 appointments so far. My rent is due the 1st and my entire income is that van. I'm scared in the specific way where you're very calm and very organized about it and that's how you know it's bad.

## Tasha — this part is for you

Tasha, I know you're about to put a deposit down with Darren. I'm not trying to make your decision for you, and I'm going to say this clearly: **this is not a hit piece.** Darren built me a van that mostly works and looks great and I'm not going to sit here and trash a guy because my battery cable melted.

But he hasn't answered three texts and one email. So I'm going to give you the facts and you can decide what to do with them. That's it. That's the whole ask.

**Before you pay any deposit, get these answers in writing. Email is fine. Text is fine. I don't care how, but I want it written down where it exists.**

1. **What gauge (AWG) is the cable on every run?** Battery to inverter, battery to battery, and anything else that carries serious current. Ask for it in writing. The number should be on the spec sheet *before* you pay, not on an invoice after.
2. **What size is the main fuse, and how far from the battery is it mounted?** Ask for both numbers.
3. **How are the battery lugs attached?** Hydraulically crimped with the correct die for the wire size, tinned lugs, terminals cleaned and treated, then tightened to spec. Ask what tool they use. If the answer is vague, that's an answer.
4. **Is the fuse sized to protect the cable, or sized to the inverter?** These are different numbers and the second one is what got me.
5. **What is the maximum continuous discharge rating on the batteries?** And how does that compare to what the inverter can pull? A 3000W inverter wants 250A. You need to know your batteries can give it, and for how long.
6. **Is my inverter 3000W continuous or 3000W peak?** I never asked this and I should have. If 3000 is the peak number, my real continuous ceiling is lower than I thought.
7. **Are the accessory circuits — dryer, water heater — individually fused?** A short in the dryer shouldn't be able to take out my whole battery bank.
8. **Where are the batteries mounted, and is that ventilation designed in?** Mine were under the bench seat in the living area. I now understand why Priya had opinions about that.
9. **Who do I call if something goes wrong, and what does the warranty actually cover?** Get the name and number of a real person.
10. **Will I be allowed to photograph and inspect the electrical work before sign-off?** If the answer is no, that's also an answer.

And the one I care about most: **if a builder balks at being asked for cable size and fuse specs in writing, walk away.** That's your answer. Nobody who does good work minds the question. People who don't want the question are the ones who mind it.

## Your own checklist — van powered off

This is the version of the list I wish someone had handed me in spring 2025. **Battery switch off. System dead. If you're not sure what you're looking at, stop and get a professional.**

**1. Find out what your inverter is actually rated for.**
Look at the label. Write down continuous watts, surge watts, and input voltage. Then write down what your dryer and water heater pull — it's usually on the label on the bottom of the unit. Add them up. Divide by 12 for 12V systems. That number is your current draw, and it's the number everything else has to support.

**2. Trace every cable from the batteries.**
Follow them with your hands, physically, all the way. Note the gauge — it's stamped on the jacket every few inches. Compare it to your draw from step 1. If a cable carrying serious current is smaller than what the load needs, that's your fire.

**3. Look at every lug and terminal with your actual eyes.**
Bad crimps show up as discoloration, a slightly melted or bubbled jacket near the terminal, a lug that moves when you wiggle it, or a terminal that's noticeably shinier or darker than the one next to it. **Heat-shrink over a lug tells you nothing.** Heat-shrink is applied to hide the joint, not to prove the joint is good. Lift it and look at the metal.

**4. Check the battery terminals for heat damage.**
Any greenish or white powdery corrosion, any discoloration, any terminal that's darker than its neighbour. Also check whether the terminals are clean copper or tinned, and whether they match the lug. Mismatched metals corrode.

**5. Find the fuse. Check the type, the rating, and the distance from the battery.**
Is it an ANL or a MIDI or a class T? What number is it? How far is it from the battery terminal — the honest answer is it should be within a foot or so, right at the battery. Then ask the critical question: **does that fuse rating make sense for the cable it's protecting?** A 300A fuse on 100A wire protects nothing.

**6. Check the cables where they pass through anything metal.**
Sheet metal edges and drilled holes will happily cut a cable's insulation. This is extremely common and I almost never think about it. Run your fingers along the full length of the cable looking for nicks, flat spots, or shiny spots. If a cable is squeezed between a panel and a bracket, it's being crushed.

**7. Look at where the batteries are mounted.**
Are they secured so they can't slide or tip? Are they in a spot with ventilation if they need it? Are they away from heat sources like a water heater or a dryer exhaust? Are the cables long enough that they're not being strained where they leave the battery?

**8. Check the inverter's clearance.**
Is there airflow around the fan vents? Is the inverter sitting in a closed cabinet? An inverter that can't breathe cooks itself.

**9. Do you have a smoke detector back there? A CO detector?**
I had the one that came with the van in the cab. My batteries were under the bench seat. If there'd been a detector back there, I'd have had a couple of minutes of warning instead of smelling plastic. **Put a smoke detector in the back of your van. Right now, today.** If you run a heater or anything that burns, get a CO detector too. This is the cheapest item on this entire list and it would have changed my whole afternoon.

**10. Know where your extinguisher is and what it's rated for.**
Mine was in the cab, which I could reach. Make sure yours is reachable from the driver's seat without opening a door. And check what it's rated for — lithium battery fires and standard fires are not the same, and there are extinguishers made for this.

**11. Practise the kill switch.**
I knew where my battery switch was. That was pure luck. Know exactly where it is, know that flipping it kills everything, and know that you can reach it. Do not go looking for it during an emergency.

**12. Photograph everything.**
Every lug, every fuse, every cable run, every battery terminal. Photos of the damage are what made my insurance claim possible, and they're what made Priya able to tell me so quickly what had happened.

## The $40 thermometer

Everyone should own a cheap infrared thermometer. I got one at Canadian Tire for $40 and it has already paid for itself several times over.

The way to use it: after you've been running your dryer and everything else for a while, point it at your lugs, your terminals, your fuse, and your cable ends. Compare them to each other. The technique isn't "is it hot" — it's "is it *hotter than the thing next to it*." A lug at 40°C when the one beside it is 25°C is a problem even though 40°C doesn't sound like a fire. A lug at 90°C is a problem regardless.

Priya's thermal camera did the same thing, just better, and the photos of her own van next to mine are the reason I understand what went wrong instead of just knowing that something did.

Two caveats. It's a surface thermometer, so it can't see inside the cable or inside a crimp — it can only tell you about the outside. And it won't save you on its own. It's a tool for noticing a developing problem, not a substitute for the build being correct.

## Where I'm at

The van's in the shop. Three weeks minimum, parts on order. Insurance adjuster comes Thursday. I've cancelled 31 appointments and I've got more to cancel before the 1st. Darren still hasn't answered my texts or my email — I've asked twice more, politely, and if he responds I'll update this post with what he says, because you should hear it from him if there's something to hear.

I'm not going to keep hammering him in public. I have a lot to be grateful for and a lot to be furious about and I'm trying to hold both of those at the same time.

What I am going to do is finish this list. I want to get a proper written spec for every wire, every fuse, every lug and every terminal on that van, with a professional's name on it, so the next version of me knows exactly what's behind the bench seat. And I'm going to get it done before I put that van back in service, not after.

If you're in the same business and you're about to pay a deposit on a build — or if you already have one and want to check it — please go do the checklist. Power off. Thirty minutes with a flashlight and a multimeter. It would have cost me nothing.

I'll post again when the van's back, with the actual repair details, what the final wiring ended up looking like, and whether anybody else in the city has had this same problem. If you have something to add, or you know something I got wrong, I genuinely want to hear it.

Go check your cables. And if you smell hot plastic, **do not** assume it's the dryer.

*No dogs were harmed. Moose had a great time.*
